en: Majjhima Nikāya 146,
Nandakovādasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, together with about five hundred bhikkhunīs, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī...
He said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One exhort the bhikkhunīs;
venerable sir, let the Blessed One instruct the bhikkhunīs.”
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One give a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhunīs.
Now at that time, the elder bhikkhus were exhorting the bhikkhunīs in turn.
The Venerable Nandaka did not wish to exhort the bhikkhunīs in turn.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, whose turn is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs in rotation?
“Venerable sir, everyone has already completed their turn to exhort the bhikkhunīs in rotation.”
“Venerable sir, this venerable Nandaka does not wish to exhort the bhikkhunīs by turn.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka:
“Exhort the bhikkhunīs, Nandaka!”
“Instruct the bhikkhunīs, Nandaka;
give a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhunīs, brahmin.
“Yes, Bhante,” the Venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. Having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after the meal, he approached the royal monastery accompanied by a single companion.
Those bhikkhunīs saw the Venerable Nandaka coming from afar;
seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing his feet.
The Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, he washed his feet.
Those bhikkhunīs, having paid homage to the Venerable Nandaka, sat down to one side.
As those bhikkhunīs were sitting to one side, the Venerable Nandaka said this to them:
"Sisters, there will be a dialogue of questions.
In that regard, those who know should say, 'We know,' and those who do not know should say, 'We do not know.'"
"Or, if anyone has any doubt or uncertainty, I myself am to be questioned on that point:
'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?'?
"Even by this much, venerable sir, we are satisfied and delighted with Master Nandaka, in that Master Nandaka invites us."
“What do you think, sisters,
is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“What do you think, sisters?”
“Is the ear permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“… Is the nose permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir. …
“Is the body permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
… “Is the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, Bhante, we have already seen this as it really is with correct wisdom:
‘In this way, these six internal sense bases are impermanent.’”
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!
For it is so, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom as it really is.
What do you think, sisters?”
“Are forms permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“What do you think, sisters,
are sounds permanent or impermanent?”
“Are scents impermanent, venerable sir, or are they permanent?
“They are impermanent, venerable sir. …
“Are tastes permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Are tactile objects permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Are phenomena permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”—
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
— “Certainly not, Bhante. — “And why is that?”
“Venerable sir, even before this we had clearly seen this as it really is with correct wisdom:
‘In this way, these six external sense bases are impermanent.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!”
"It is indeed so, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom according to reality.
What do you think, sisters,
is eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent?"
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“What do you think, sisters, is ear-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“… Is nose-consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Is tongue-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir. …
“Is body-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Is mind-consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, Bhante, we have already previously seen this as it really is with correct wisdom:
‘In this way, these six classes of consciousness are impermanent.’”
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!
For it is so, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom as it really is.

Sisters, it is just as when an oil lamp is burning: the oil is impermanent and subject to change; the wick is impermanent and subject to change; the flame is impermanent and subject to change; and the light is impermanent and subject to change.”
Sisters, if someone were to say this:
"Of that burning oil lamp, the oil is impermanent and subject to change; the wick is impermanent and subject to change; the flame is impermanent and subject to change;
but its radiance is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change."
“Would he, sisters, be speaking rightly if he were to say this?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“And for what reason?”
“Venerable sir, for that burning oil lamp, the oil is impermanent and subject to change; the wick is impermanent and subject to change; the flame is impermanent and subject to change;
how much more so its radiance, which is impermanent and subject to change.
“In the same way, sisters, if anyone were to say this:”
"‘The six internal sense bases are impermanent,
but whatever pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure one experiences in dependence upon the six internal sense bases is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’—
would he, sisters, be speaking rightly if he were to say this?"
“No, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, various feelings arise in dependence upon various corresponding conditions.”
“With the cessation of this and that specific condition, this and that specific feeling ceases.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!
For it is so, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom according to reality.”
Just as, sisters, for a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, the root is impermanent and subject to change,
the trunk is impermanent and subject to change, the branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change, and even the shadow is impermanent and subject to change.
Sisters, if anyone were to say this:
“Of that great tree standing here, possessed of heartwood, even the root is impermanent and subject to change;
the trunk is impermanent and subject to change; the branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change; and whatever of it—”
“‘That shadow is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’—
would he, sisters, be speaking rightly if he were to say this?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And for what reason?

“Because, Bhante, of that great tree standing possessed of heartwood, even the root is impermanent and subject to change; the trunk is impermanent and subject to change; the branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change;
how much more so its shadow, which is impermanent and subject to change.”
“In the same way, sisters, if anyone were to say:
‘These six external sense bases are impermanent;

but whatever pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure one experiences in dependence upon these six external sense bases—that is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’—[that would be wrong].”
“Sisters, would he be speaking rightly if he were to say this?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“And for what reason?”
“Venerable sir, specific feelings arise dependent upon specific conditions.
With the cessation of those specific conditions, those specific feelings cease.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!”
For it is thus, sisters, that it happens for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom as it really is.

Sisters, it is just as if a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, were to carve it up with a sharp carving knife without cutting through the inner mass of flesh or the outer layer of hide.
Whatever internal flesh, sinew, or binding tissue there might be in that cow, one would cut it away, slice it, hack it, and carve it with a sharp butcher’s knife.
Having cut, sliced, hacked, and carved it away, and having shaken off the outer hide, one would cover that cow with that very hide and say:
“This cow is joined with this very hide.”
“Sisters, would he be speaking rightly if he were to say that?
“Certainly not, venerable sir. “And why is that?”

“Venerable sir, suppose a skilled butcher or his apprentice were to kill a cow and, with a sharp carving knife, were to cut it apart without damaging the inner mass of flesh and without damaging the outer hide.
Whatever internal soft flesh, sinew, or binding tissue there might be, he would cut, sever, slice, and carve each of those away with the sharp carving knife.
“Having cut it up, having hacked it, having carved it, having sliced it, and having shaken off the outer hide, and then covering that cow with that very hide— even if he were to say,
‘This cow is still joined with this very hide,’ yet that cow would nonetheless be disjoined from that hide.”
“Sisters, this simile has been used by me for the purpose of making the meaning known.
This is the meaning here:
‘The mass of flesh within,’ sisters, is a designation for these six internal sense bases.”
“‘The outer hide,’ sisters, is a designation for these six external sense bases.
‘The inner flesh, the inner sinews, the inner ligaments,’ sisters, is a designation for delight and lust.
‘The sharp butcher’s knife,’ sisters, is a designation for noble wisdom.”
This noble wisdom cuts through, cleaves, splits, and completely shatters the underlying afflictions, the fetters, and the bonds within.
Furthermore, sisters, there are these seven factors of enlightenment;

by developing and cultivating them, a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
He enters upon and dwells in them.
Which seven?
Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena … [as before] … he develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture …
He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility… he develops the enlightenment factor of concentration… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
“Sisters, these are the seven factors of enlightenment, by the development and cultivation of which a bhikkhu,
through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself with direct knowledge in this very life.”
Then the Venerable Nandaka, having exhorted those bhikkhunīs with this instruction, dismissed them, saying:
"Go, sisters; it is time.
Then those bhikkhunīs, having rejoiced and expressed their appreciation for the Venerable Nandaka’s words, rose from their seats.
Having paid homage to the Venerable Nandaka and circumambulated him, they approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side. As they were standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhunīs:
“Go, bhikkhunīs; it is time.
Then those bhikkhunīs, having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, departed.
Not long after they had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, just as on the fourteenth day of the uposatha, most people have neither doubt nor uncertainty as to whether the moon is waning or waxing,
yet it is simply understood that the moon is waning;
even so, bhikkhus, those bhikkhunīs were uplifted by Nandaka’s teaching of the Dhamma, yet their aspirations were not fulfilled.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Nandaka:
“In that case, Nandaka, you should exhort those bhikkhunīs tomorrow with that same exhortation.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One.
Then, when that night had passed, the Venerable Nandaka dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, he returned from his almsround after the meal and, accompanied by a single companion, approached the royal monastery.
Those bhikkhunīs saw the Venerable Nandaka coming from afar.
Having seen him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing his feet.
The Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat and washed his feet.
Then those bhikkhunīs, having paid homage to the Venerable Nandaka, sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, the Venerable Nandaka said this to them:
“Sisters, this will be a discourse by way of questions.”
In that case, those who understand should say, "We understand," and those who do not understand should say, "We do not understand.
Or, if anyone has doubt or uncertainty, I myself should be questioned on that point:
"Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?"
“Venerable sir, we are indeed gratified and pleased that the noble Nandaka invites us for the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
“What do you think, sisters, is the eye permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”—
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“What do you think, sisters, is the ear permanent or impermanent?”
“Is the nose impermanent, venerable sir, or is it permanent? “It is impermanent, venerable sir. […] “Is the nose impermanent or permanent?
“It is impermanent, venerable sir. […]
“Is the tongue … the body … the mind permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, Bhante, we have already seen this as it really is with correct wisdom:
‘In this way, these six internal sense bases are impermanent.’”
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!
For it is so, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom as it really is.
What do you think, sisters, are forms permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“What do you think, sisters, are sounds permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“… Are odors permanent or impermanent? [The same response.]
“Impermanent, venerable sir… Are tastes permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.”...
“Are tactile objects permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.
“… Are mental phenomena permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, Bhante, we have already seen this as it really is with correct wisdom:
‘In this way, these six external sense bases are impermanent.’”
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!
For it is thus, sisters, that it is for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom as it really is.
What do you think, sisters, is eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Is ear-consciousness, venerable sir, permanent or impermanent? “It is impermanent, venerable sir. […] “Is ear-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“It is impermanent, venerable sir.”
“Is nose-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“Is tongue-consciousness permanent or impermanent?”
“Is body-consciousness, venerable sir, permanent or impermanent?
“It is impermanent, venerable sir.”
“Is mind-consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, Bhante.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, we have already seen this as it really is with correct wisdom:”
“Thus these six classes of consciousness are impermanent.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!
For it is so, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom according to reality.”

"Just as, sisters, when an oil lamp is burning, the oil is impermanent and subject to change, the wick is impermanent and subject to change, the flame is impermanent and subject to change, and the light is impermanent and subject to change—what do you think, sisters, if someone were to say:

‘Of this burning oil lamp, the oil is impermanent and subject to change, the wick is impermanent and subject to change, the flame is impermanent and subject to change’; [would that person be speaking correctly?]"
"And that radiance of his is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change"—
would he be speaking rightly, sisters, if he were to say this?
"Certainly not, venerable sir."
“And what is the reason for that?
“Because, Bhante, while that oil lamp is burning, the oil is impermanent and subject to change, the wick is impermanent and subject to change, and the flame is impermanent and subject to change;
how much more so its radiance, which is certainly impermanent and subject to change.”
“In the same way, sisters, if anyone were to say:
‘These six internal sense bases are impermanent,

but whatever pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure one experiences in dependence upon these six internal sense bases— that is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’— [that would be wrong].”
“Sisters, would he be speaking rightly if he were to say this?
“Certainly not, Bhante. “And why is that?”
“Venerable sir, various feelings arise dependent on various respective conditions;
with the cessation of various respective conditions, various feelings cease.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!”
Thus it is, sisters, for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom according to reality.
Sisters, just as for a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, the root is impermanent and subject to change,
the trunk is impermanent and subject to change, the branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change, and even the shadow—
They are impermanent and subject to change.
Sisters, if someone were to say this:

‘Of that great tree standing there, possessed of heartwood, the root is impermanent and subject to change, the trunk is impermanent and subject to change, and the branches and foliage are also impermanent and subject to change;’
“And as for his shadow, would it be permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante. “Sisters, would he be speaking rightly if he were to say that?”—
“No indeed, Bhante.”
“And for what reason?

“Because, Bhante, of that great tree standing possessed of heartwood, even the root is impermanent and subject to change; the trunk is impermanent and subject to change; the branches and foliage are impermanent and subject to change;
how much more so its shadow, which is impermanent and subject to change.”
“In the same way, sisters, if someone were to say:
‘These six external sense bases are impermanent,

but whatever pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure one experiences in dependence upon these external sense bases— that is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’— [that would be incorrect].”
“Sisters, would one speaking rightly speak thus?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“And for what reason?”
“Dependent upon this or that specific condition, bhante, this or that specific feeling arises.
With the cessation of this or that specific condition, this or that specific feeling ceases.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters!”
For it is thus, sisters, that it is for a noble disciple who sees with right wisdom according to reality.

Sisters, it is just as if a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, were to carve it up with a sharp butcher’s knife, cutting through the cow without piercing the inner mass of flesh and without piercing the outer hide.
Whatever internal flesh, sinew, or binding there might be, one would cut it away, sever it, hack it, and slice it with a sharp butcher’s knife.
Having cut it away, severed it, hacked it, and sliced it, and having shaken off the outer hide, one would cover that cow with that very hide and say:
“This cow is joined with this very hide.”
“Sisters, would he be speaking rightly if he were to speak thus?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“And for what reason?”
“Venerable sir, suppose a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, were to cut it up with a sharp butcher’s knife so as to sever the inner flesh without piercing the outer hide,
and whatever internal flesh, sinew, or ligament there might be, he would cut, sever, slice, and carve that very thing away with the sharp butcher’s knife.”
“Having cut it off, having sliced it, having carved it, having carved it all around, and having shaken off the outer hide, if one were to cover that cow with that very hide and say:
‘This cow is still joined with this very hide,’ yet that cow would nonetheless be disjoined from that hide.”
“Sisters, this simile has been employed by me for the sake of making the meaning known; this is its meaning here:
‘The inner mass of flesh,’ sisters, is a designation for the six internal sense bases;
‘the outer skin,’ sisters, is a designation for the six external sense bases.”
“‘Meat between,’ ‘sinew between,’ and ‘binding between,’ sisters, is a designation for delight-and-lust.
‘A sharp butcher’s knife,’ sisters, is a designation for noble wisdom—
that noble wisdom which cuts through, hacks away, chops up, and carves out the defilement between, the fetter between, and the bond between.”
Furthermore, sisters, there are these seven factors of enlightenment, by the development and cultivation of which a bhikkhu,
through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself with direct knowledge in this very life.
Which seven?
Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He develops the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment … [and so on] … [as before].
He develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture … he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility …

He develops the concentration factor of enlightenment … he develops the equanimity factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment. Sisters,
these are the seven factors of enlightenment, by the development and cultivation of which a bhikkhu [is freed from the taints].
“Through its destruction, he dwells, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
having entered upon them.
Then the Venerable Nandaka, having exhorted those bhikkhunīs with this instruction, dismissed them.
“Go, sisters; it is time.

Then those bhikkhunīs, having rejoiced and expressed their appreciation for the Venerable Nandaka’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Venerable Nandaka, and keeping him to their right, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
As they were standing there, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhunīs:
“Go, bhikkhunīs; it is time.”
Then those bhikkhunīs, having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, departed.
Not long after those bhikkhunīs had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, just as on the fifteenth day of the uposatha, there is no doubt or perplexity among many people regarding [the moon]:"
“Is the moon deficient, or is the moon full?”—it is simply that the moon is full.
In the same way, monks, those bhikkhunīs were uplifted by Nandaka’s teaching of the Dhamma and their aspirations were fulfilled.

Among those five hundred bhikkhunīs, monks, even the one who was the last [to attain] became a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as her final goal.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Nandakovāda Sutta, the fourth, is finished.
